extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of poetry and drama (poets, playwrights, literary critics) studying Aristotelian poetics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative principles drawn from Aristotle's Art of Poetry (with commentary) about what makes good tragedy, comedy, epic, and their performance — covering plot, diction, verse, chorus, actors, and staging. Useful for analysing or composing dramatic and epic poetry per classical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greater genius required for praise than for slander
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle: 'there is requir'd a greater Genius to Praiſe, than to Slander.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who compose hymns and panegyrics must be more grave and lofty in tone and capacity than those who write raillery or satire, which are lower and debased. This is an evaluative standard for judging the seriousness and dignity of subjects and their required poetic ability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate verse-form to subject (iambic for invective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Iambic poems are 'nothing elſe but Continual Invective' and iambizein 'signifies to ſpeak Inju riouſly.' Iambic verse is the most proper for raillery and invective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match metrical form to content: use iambics for satirical/raillery material; heroic and panegyric themes demand loftier measures. The name 'iambic' was applied where the verse form suited the invective purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heroic/tragic subject demands elevated genius and manner
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragic and heroic poems treat the actions of gods and heroes and require an elevated, noble style; Homer 'had the most elevated Genius' and applied himself to grave and serious matters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge heroic/tragic works by the nobility of subject and loftiness of style; authors should employ elevated diction and management of subject (action, catastrophe, mixture of elements) appropriate to greatness of theme.

rubrics_metrics.name: A poet must produce dramatic imitation (theatrical imitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Aristotle praises Homer because he 'made Dramatic Imitations' — not only wrote well but invented ideas of tragedy and comedy through imitation of action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being 'a poet' entails the capacity to create imitative actions (plots) that present characters and events in a manner fit for dramatic representation, not merely fine writing. Evaluate poets on their ability to shape action, disposition, and management.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspects of tragedy to examine: fable, manners, diction, plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy should be examined 'in respect to it self ... to know whether that which properly Conſtitutes its Eſſence, be perfectly good, as the Fable, the Manners, the Diction and the Plot.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or constructing tragedy, attend to the unity and quality of the fable (story), the truth and suitability of characters' manners, the appropriateness and artistry of diction, and the arrangement of the plot. These are core internal criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate tragedy in respect to the theatre (representation and spectacle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy must also be judged 'in respect to the Theatre, to know, if no new Beauties can be added to the Decoration, and Muſick, and ... whether the Repreſentation anſwers ſo exactly to the Action.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether staging, decorations, music and other performative elements enhance the imitation and whether the representation corresponds exactly to the action so that nothing is lacking to render the imitation more perfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of action preserved through the principal character
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduction of additional actors obliged one to form 'the Principal Character' so that unity of action is preserved: one actor must hold the chief part while others are subordinate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To maintain unity and focus, designate a principal character whose central purpose organizes the plot; subordinate roles should support that unity rather than compete with it for parity of importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the number of speaking persons per scene (three ideal)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophocles 'added a third Actor' and the Greek tragedians 'remain'd here, and never thought of increaſing the Number,' with the remark 'Neer ſtrive to make a fourth Perſon ſpeak.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep concurrent speakers to three where possible: three-person dialogue is clearest and most natural; introducing a fourth risks confusion unless handled with exceptional skill and purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and proportion of the Chorus: subordinate, shortened songs
rubrics_metrics.description: Originally chorus dominated, but 'Aſchylus ... ſhorten'd the Songs of the Chorus' so that chorus serves to give respite to actors and should not overwhelm the dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus as a supporting, intermittent element rather than the principal narrator; keep choral odes proportionate to the dramatic needs and avoid allowing them to obstruct dialogue and action. (Also note historical regulation reducing chorus size—practical performance constraint.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage-decoration must accord exactly with subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Sophocles 'chang'd the Decorations, according to his Subjects, and tis this makes the Ornament of the Scene, when it agrees exact: with what it repreſents.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure scenery, altars, tombs, and machines visually and functionally fit the subject and action of the piece; congruence between representation and subject enhances verisimilitude and artistic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of costume and stagecraft to confer majesty; avoid onstage blood
rubrics_metrics.description: Æschylus 'found for this Art ... Robes and Masks' and 'firſt Spoke ſublime.' He is said also to have 'first thought it indecent, to ſprinkle the Scenes with blood' and removed murders from the spectators' eyes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ masks, robes, elevated footwear (buskins) and other costuming to raise the dignity of characters; handle violent acts offstage to preserve decency and the audience's sensibilities, using stagecraft rather than spectacle of gore.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verse-form must suit style and dramatic function
rubrics_metrics.description: Tetrameter was used for satyrical/dancing chorus because it suits motion; tragedy adopted trimeter iambic because it most resembles ordinary discourse; hexameters used rarely when passing 'the bounds of ordinary Vicſcourſe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose metrical form by function: tetrameter for movement and dance, trimeter iambic for natural-sounding dialogue in tragedy, hexameter for elevated, sonorous passages. The verse should imitate the natural tone of the intended speech or effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes and the composition of parts should be natural and proper
rubrics_metrics.description: The number of episodes 'encreaſed alſo with Time' and episodes were combined into natural parts 'which however were natural and proper to the Subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct episodes so they cohere and arise naturally from the action; avoid artificial concatenation—each episode should serve the subject and fit organically into the whole structure of the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of comedy: imitation of the ridiculous (not of cruelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy is 'an Imitation of the worſt Men' in the sense of ridicule: 'Ridicule is properly Defect, and Deformity without Pain, and ... never contributes to the Deſtruction of his Subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select comic subjects that expose folly, defect or deformity in a way that excites laughter, not pity or horror. Avoid making pain or destructive suffering the object of comedic ridicule; ridicule should not derive from cruelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy must not arouse pity, horror, or serious indignation
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy 'banisnes all that can cauſe Horror, Averſion, or Pity, as alſo what is too ſerious or ſevere from his Comick Theatre.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing or judging comedy, exclude subjects whose emotional weight would provoke pity, disgust, or moral outrage; comic treatment requires lighter, ridicule-appropriate material unless expertly blended with humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy may expose eminent persons only by reduction to ridicule
rubrics_metrics.description: While comedies sometimes introduce eminent citizens and magistrates, doing so must be in the service of ridicule: 'it is a true Comedy, where he turns the Subject of Tragedy into Ridicule.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If high-status characters appear in comedy, they should be treated so as to produce comic effect (ridicule), not to elevate dignity; the majesty of princes is generally incompatible with pure comedy unless deliberately subverted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judgement transfer between tragedy and epic
rubrics_metrics.description: He that can 'judge well of a Tragedy ... can alſo judge of Epoſeia, for all the parts of Epopoeia are found in Tragedy; but all thoſe of Tragedy are not found in Epopoeia.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize overlap: mastery in assessing tragedy supports assessment of epic narrative (epopeia), because tragedy contains many elements of epic. Use knowledge of tragic components (plot, diction, character) when evaluating epic works.
